29492.e: Israel lies at the eastern end of the Mediterranean. Independence was proclaimed in 1948 in the coastal city of Tel Aviv.

29493.q: Which organisation approved a plan to divide Palestine in November 1947?
29493.e: The UN Partition Plan provided for a Jewish and an Arab state, with Jerusalem under international administration. The Arab side rejected the plan.
29493.m: In 1947 the UN approved a partition plan for Palestine.

29494.q: Which religion do most people in Israel belong to?
29494.e: Israel was founded in 1948 as a Jewish state. Most of its inhabitants are Jewish, and many Muslims and Christians also live there.
29494.m: Most people in Israel are Jewish.

29495.q: What happened immediately after Israel was founded in May 1948?
29495.e: Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon attacked the new state. In the Palestine war hundreds of thousands of Palestinians fled or were driven out.
29495.m: The founding of the state in 1948 was followed by a war.

29496.q: In which year did Mao Zedong proclaim the People’s Republic of China?
29496.e: On 1 October 1949 Mao announced the founding of the People’s Republic in Beijing. Before that the communists had won the civil war.
29496.m: The People’s Republic of China has existed since 1949.

29497.q: In which square in Beijing did Mao proclaim the People’s Republic in 1949?
29497.e: Mao spoke from the Gate of Heavenly Peace, the Tiananmen. A large portrait of him still hangs there today.
29497.m: Mao proclaimed the People’s Republic in Tiananmen Square.

29498.q: Which party did Mao’s communists fight against in the Chinese Civil War?
29498.e: The nationalist Kuomintang under Chiang Kai-shek governed China before 1949. It lost the civil war to the communists.
29498.m: Mao defeated the Kuomintang in the civil war.

29499.q: To which island did the defeated Kuomintang government withdraw in 1949?
29499.e: Chiang Kai-shek fled to Taiwan with his government. The Republic of China still exists there today.
29499.m: The Kuomintang government fled to Taiwan in 1949.

29500.q: What is the name of the retreat of the Chinese communists over thousands of kilometres in 1934 and 1935?
29500.e: On the Long March the communists covered about 12,000 kilometres. During it Mao became the leading figure of the party.
29500.m: On the Long March Mao rose to become leader.

29501.q: What was the name of Mao’s campaign from 1958 that led to one of the worst famines in history?
29501.e: China was supposed to catch up with Western industry in a short time. Bad planning led to a famine with many millions of deaths.
29501.m: The Great Leap Forward ended in famine.

29502.q: What is the name of the movement from 1966 in which Red Guards went after supposed enemies of Mao?
29502.e: In the Cultural Revolution teachers, artists and party members were persecuted, and cultural treasures were destroyed. It lasted until Mao’s death in 1976.
29502.m: The Cultural Revolution brought China great suffering from 1966.

29503.q: Compared with other Western countries, when did Switzerland recognise the People’s Republic of China?
a: Very early, as one of the first
Only as one of the last
29503.e: Switzerland recognised the People’s Republic of China as early as 17 January 1950. This made it one of the first Western countries to do so.
29503.m: Switzerland recognised the People’s Republic of China as early as 1950.

29504.q: How was the Korean War ended in 1953?
29504.e: The fighting was stopped in 1953 by an armistice agreement. To this day there is no peace treaty.
29504.m: The Korean War ended only with a ceasefire.

29505.q: Which US general led the UN troops in Korea in 1950?
29505.e: Douglas MacArthur was commander-in-chief of the UN troops. He was dismissed by President Truman in 1951 because he wanted to extend the war to China.
29505.m: Douglas MacArthur led the UN troops in Korea.

29506.q: Which country sent hundreds of thousands of soldiers to support North Korea from autumn 1950?
29506.e: When the UN troops advanced to the Chinese border, the People’s Republic of China stepped in with so-called volunteers. After that the front ran through the middle of Korea again.
29506.m: In 1950 China entered the war on North Korea’s side.

29507.q: Which part of Korea did the UN troops support in the Korean War?
29507.e: The Security Council condemned the attack from the north and called for help for South Korea. Most of the UN soldiers came from the USA.
29507.m: The UN troops fought for South Korea.

29508.q: Who was the ruler of North Korea during the Korean War?
29508.e: Kim Il-sung led North Korea from 1948 until his death in 1994. His family still rules the country today.
29508.m: Kim Il-sung founded North Korea’s ruling family.

29509.q: What is the name of the strip of border about four kilometres wide between North and South Korea?
29509.e: The Demilitarised Zone was created with the ceasefire. It is about 4 kilometres wide and about 250 kilometres long.
29509.m: Korea is still divided by the Demilitarised Zone.

29510.q: Which capital was captured four times in the Korean War?
29510.e: Seoul was captured four times during the war, first by one side and then by the other. The city was badly destroyed.
29510.m: Seoul was captured four times in the Korean War.

29511.q: In which year did the popular uprising in Hungary take place?
29511.e: The uprising began on 23 October and was crushed by Soviet troops at the beginning of November.
29511.m: The Hungarian Uprising was in autumn 1956.

29512.q: Which power crushed the Hungarian Uprising with tanks?
29512.e: From 4 November 1956 the Soviet army moved into Budapest. Thousands of people died.
29512.m: Soviet tanks ended the uprising in Hungary.

29513.q: Who governed Hungary after the uprising was crushed in 1956?
a: A government backed by the Soviet Union
A government backed by the USA
29513.e: The Soviet Union put János Kádár in place as the new leader. He remained head of the party until 1988.
29513.m: After 1956 Hungary stayed under Soviet influence.

29514.q: How did Switzerland respond to many people fleeing Hungary in 1956?
29514.e: Switzerland took in the Hungarian refugees without long individual checks, and the population was very willing to help. In total about 14,000 people came.
29514.m: Switzerland took in many Hungarian refugees in 1956.

29515.q: Which monument did demonstrators pull down on the first day of the uprising in Budapest?
29515.e: On 23 October 1956 people pulled a huge statue of Stalin in Budapest off its base. It became the symbol of the uprising.
29515.m: The fall of the Stalin monument became the image of the uprising.

29516.q: Which other crisis distracted the West’s attention from Hungary in autumn 1956?
29516.e: At the same time Great Britain, France and Israel attacked Egypt at the Suez Canal. As a result the Western powers were divided and distracted.
29516.m: The Suez Crisis happened at the same time as the Hungarian Uprising.

29517.q: How did Switzerland protest in 1956 against the crushing of the uprising in Hungary?
a: It stayed away from the Olympic Games
It declared war on the Soviet Union
It closed its borders to Hungarians
29517.e: Switzerland, the Netherlands and Spain stayed away from the 1956 Summer Games in Melbourne in protest. At that time Switzerland was not even a member of the UN.
29517.m: Because of Hungary, Switzerland missed the 1956 Olympic Games.

29518.q: What was the barrier mainly made of in the first days after 13 August 1961?
29518.e: First soldiers and police ran barbed wire through the city. Only in the following days did they start building a wall of stone and concrete.
29518.m: At first it was mainly barbed wire that divided the city.

29519.q: What did the young East German border guard Conrad Schumann do in a world-famous photo in August 1961?
a: He jumped over the barbed wire to the West.
He knocked down the Wall with a hammer.
He raised a flag on the Wall.
29519.e: On 15 August 1961 Conrad Schumann jumped over the barbed wire to West Berlin on Bernauer Strasse. A photographer captured the jump, and the picture went around the world.
29519.m: The photo of Conrad Schumann’s jump to the West is world-famous.

29520.q: What was the guarded area between the walls called, where people trying to escape were shot at?
29520.e: Between the inner and outer walls there was a strip with watchtowers, lights and barriers. Because people trying to escape were shot at there, it was called the death strip.
29520.m: The death strip made escape extremely dangerous.

29521.q: How can you tell in many places in Berlin today where the Wall used to stand?
a: By a double row of cobblestones in the ground
29521.e: A double row of cobblestones shows the course of the former Wall through the city. On Bernauer Strasse there is also the Berlin Wall Memorial.
29521.m: Cobblestones in the ground show where the Berlin Wall stood.

29522.q: What is the name of the longest surviving section of the Berlin Wall, which artists have painted?
29522.e: The East Side Gallery on the Spree is about 1.3 kilometres long. In 1990 more than 100 artists painted the Wall.
29522.m: The East Side Gallery is the longest painted section of the Wall.

29523.q: How did 57 people escape under the Wall to West Berlin in 1964?
29523.e: Students dug a tunnel from West Berlin to beneath a house in East Berlin. It was later called “Tunnel 57”.

29524.q: What happened at Checkpoint Charlie in October 1961?
a: US and Soviet tanks faced each other
29524.e: After a dispute about checks, American and Soviet tanks drove up and stood directly facing each other on 27 and 28 October 1961. After about 16 hours both sides withdrew.
29524.m: At Checkpoint Charlie in 1961 the superpowers’ tanks faced each other.

29525.q: Who was head of government of the Soviet Union during the Cuban Missile Crisis?
29525.e: Nikita Khrushchev secretly had missiles placed in Cuba. He led the Soviet Union from 1953 to 1964.
29525.m: Khrushchev was the Soviet opponent in the Cuban Missile Crisis.

29526.q: Who was US president during the Cuban Missile Crisis?
29526.e: John F. Kennedy was president from 1961 until he was assassinated in 1963. During the Cuban Missile Crisis he met with a crisis team every day.
29526.m: Kennedy led the USA through the Cuban Missile Crisis.

29527.q: Roughly how long did the most dangerous phase of the Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962 last?
29527.e: From 16 to 28 October 1962 the world was on the brink of nuclear war. That is why people also speak of the “thirteen days”.
29527.m: The Cuban Missile Crisis lasted thirteen tense days.

29528.q: With which spy plane did the USA photograph the missile bases in Cuba?
29528.e: The U-2 flew at a very great height and took detailed aerial photos. During the crisis a U-2 was shot down over Cuba.
29528.m: Photos from a U-2 plane set off the Cuban Missile Crisis.

29529.q: In which year did Fidel Castro come to power in Cuba?
29529.e: At the beginning of 1959 Castro’s revolutionaries overthrew the dictator Fulgencio Batista. After that Cuba moved closer to the Soviet Union.
29529.m: Castro ruled Cuba from the revolution of 1959.

29530.q: Roughly how far is Cuba from the coast of Florida?
29530.e: Only about 150 kilometres of sea lie between Cuba and the Florida Keys. Missiles in Cuba could have reached large parts of the USA in a few minutes.
29530.m: Cuba is very close to the USA.

29531.q: Which treaty did the USA, the Soviet Union and Great Britain sign in 1963, one year after the Cuban Missile Crisis?
a: A treaty to stop many nuclear tests
A treaty to found the UN
29531.e: The Test Ban Treaty of 1963 banned nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in space and under water. Underground tests were still allowed.
29531.m: After the Cuban Missile Crisis many nuclear tests were banned in 1963.

29532.q: From which spaceport was Sputnik 1 launched?
29532.e: Sputnik 1 was launched in 1957 from the Baikonur Cosmodrome on the steppe of Kazakhstan. Russia still launches many rockets from there today.
29532.m: Sputnik 1 flew into space from Baikonur.

29533.q: What had the rocket that took Sputnik 1 into space actually been built for?
29533.e: The R-7 had been built as an intercontinental missile for nuclear weapons. A modified version put Sputnik into orbit.
29533.m: Sputnik 1 flew into space on a converted military rocket.

29534.q: How did the USA react to the launch of Sputnik 1?
a: They soon sent their own satellite into space
They gave up space travel completely
They bought Sputnik from the Soviet Union
They brought Sputnik down from the sky
29534.e: The USA did not want to fall behind. On 31 January 1958 their first satellite, Explorer 1, was launched.
29534.m: Sputnik started a race into space.

29535.q: How long did Sputnik 1 send radio signals to Earth?
29535.e: After about 21 days the batteries ran out and the transmitter went silent. The satellite then orbited the Earth silently for several more weeks.
29535.m: Sputnik 1 transmitted for only about three weeks.

29536.q: How old was Yuri Gagarin when he flew into space in 1961?
29536.e: Gagarin was born on 9 March 1934. So on his space flight he was 27 years old.
29536.m: Gagarin was only 27 when he flew into space.

29537.q: How did Yuri Gagarin die in 1968?
a: In the crash of a training aircraft
29537.e: Gagarin died on 27 March 1968 on a training flight in a jet fighter. He was only 34 years old.
29537.m: Gagarin died in a plane crash in 1968.

29539.q: How many times did Yuri Gagarin orbit the Earth on his space flight in 1961?
29539.e: Gagarin’s flight lasted only 108 minutes. In this time he went around the Earth once and then landed again.

29541.q: From which city was the flight of Apollo 11 monitored by ground control?
29541.e: NASA’s control centre is in Houston, Texas. That is why the first message from the Moon began with “Houston”.
29541.m: Ground control for the Moon flights was in Houston.

29542.q: Roughly how long did the whole Apollo 11 mission last?
29542.e: Apollo 11 launched on 16 July 1969 and returned on 24 July. The mission lasted a little over 8 days.
29542.m: Apollo 11 was on its way for about eight days.

29543.q: What did the Apollo 11 astronauts have to do after returning to Earth?
a: Stay in quarantine for three weeks
Stay in hospital for a year
29543.e: No one knew for sure whether there were germs on the Moon. That is why the astronauts were kept apart for about 21 days.
29543.m: After the Moon flight the astronauts went into quarantine.

29544.q: Which device did the Apollo 11 astronauts set up that is still used to measure the distance to the Moon?
29544.e: From Earth, laser beams are sent to the reflector, and the time until the light returns is measured. In this way the distance is known to within a few centimetres.
29544.m: A laser reflector on the Moon helps measure the distance precisely.

29545.q: How many people in total walked on the Moon in the Apollo programme?
29545.e: Between 1969 and 1972 six Apollo missions landed on the Moon, each with two astronauts on the surface. So there were 12 people altogether.
29545.m: Twelve people in total have stood on the Moon.

29546.q: With which mission did people last land on the Moon in 1972?
29546.e: Apollo 17 landed on the Moon in December 1972. No one has been there since.
29546.m: Since Apollo 17 in 1972 nobody has been on the Moon.

29547.q: Which great power fought with hundreds of thousands of soldiers on the side of South Vietnam?
29547.e: From 1965 the USA sent combat troops to Vietnam, at times over 500,000 soldiers. They wanted to prevent the whole of Vietnam from becoming communist.
29547.m: The USA fought for South Vietnam in the Vietnam War.

29548.q: Who was the leader of North Vietnam and the Vietnamese communists?
29548.e: Ho Chi Minh first fought against the French colonial rulers and then led North Vietnam. He died in 1969, before the end of the war.
29548.m: Ho Chi Minh was the leader of North Vietnam.

29549.q: What were the communist fighters in South Vietnam called?
29549.e: The Viet Cong fought a guerrilla war from the jungle and from tunnel systems. It was supported by North Vietnam.
29549.m: The Viet Cong fighters waged a guerrilla war.

29550.q: Which city was the capital of North Vietnam?
29550.e: Hanoi in the north was the seat of North Vietnam’s government. Since reunification in 1976 it has been the capital of all Vietnam.
29550.m: Hanoi was the capital of North Vietnam.

29551.q: How did the Vietnam War end in 1975?
a: France took over the country again
29551.e: After the US troops left in 1973, North Vietnam captured Saigon in 1975. A year later Vietnam was reunited as a communist state.
29551.m: In 1975 North Vietnam conquered the south.

29552.q: Which colonial power was defeated at Dien Bien Phu in Vietnam in 1954?
29552.e: The defeat at Dien Bien Phu ended French colonial rule in Indochina. After that Vietnam was divided for the time being.
29552.m: At Dien Bien Phu France lost its colony of Vietnam.

29553.q: How did many people in the USA and Europe react to the Vietnam War?
a: They called for a nuclear attack
They sent troops to North Vietnam
29553.e: Pictures of destruction and death came into people’s living rooms through television. Young people in particular protested against the war around the world.
29553.m: There were huge protests against the Vietnam War around the world.

29554.q: In which year did the Prague Spring take place?
29554.e: From January 1968 the leadership of Czechoslovakia tried to make socialism freer. In August the attempt was ended by force.

29555.q: In which present-day country is Prague, the city of the Prague Spring?
29555.e: Prague was the capital of Czechoslovakia. In 1993 the country split, and today Prague is the capital of the Czech Republic.
29555.m: Prague is the capital of the Czech Republic.

29556.q: Which slogan described the aim of the Prague Spring?
29556.e: The reformers did not want to abolish socialism, but to make it freer and fairer. That is what this slogan stood for.
29556.m: The Prague Spring wanted socialism with a human face.

29557.q: How was the Prague Spring ended in August 1968?
29557.e: On the night of 20 to 21 August 1968 hundreds of thousands of soldiers from several Eastern Bloc countries invaded. The reforms were then reversed.
29557.m: Warsaw Pact tanks ended the Prague Spring.

29558.q: How did Switzerland respond to many people fleeing Czechoslovakia in 1968?
a: It took in thousands of refugees
It broke off contact with Europe
29558.e: After the invasion many Czechs and Slovaks came to Switzerland. They were taken in without long individual checks.
29558.m: In 1968 Switzerland helped refugees from Czechoslovakia.

29559.q: Which country led the invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968?
29559.e: The Soviet Union would not tolerate the reforms. Its troops invaded together with soldiers from other Eastern Bloc countries.
29559.m: The Soviet Union ended the Prague Spring by force.

29560.q: What was largely lifted during the Prague Spring?
29560.e: In 1968 newspapers, radio and television could report openly and voice criticism. After the invasion censorship was brought back.
29560.m: During the Prague Spring the media could report freely.

29561.q: Who led the GDR from 1971 until October 1989?
29561.e: Erich Honecker was General Secretary of the SED and head of state. In autumn 1989 he had to resign under pressure from the protests.
29561.m: Erich Honecker ruled the GDR until shortly before the fall of the Wall.

29562.q: Which chant became a sign of the wish for reunification after the fall of the Wall?
29562.e: From the end of 1989 many demonstrators chanted “We are one people”. With this they demanded the unity of East and West Germany.
29562.m: With “We are one people” unity was demanded.

29563.q: Which small East German car became a symbol of the opening of the border in 1989?
29563.e: After the border opened, long lines of “Trabis” drove to the West. The car had a body made of plastic.
29563.m: The Trabi is a symbol of the end of East Germany.

29564.q: What were the people called who chipped pieces off the Wall with hammers and chisels after it fell?
29564.e: Many people wanted a piece of the Wall as a souvenir. Because they tapped away like woodpeckers, they were called “Mauerspechte”, wall woodpeckers.
29564.m: Wall woodpeckers took souvenirs from the Wall.

29565.q: In which East German city did the big Monday demonstrations begin in 1989?
29565.e: Every Monday people met in Leipzig’s St Nicholas Church for prayers for peace. In autumn 1989 thousands of them then marched through the city.
29565.m: The Monday demonstrations began in Leipzig.

29566.q: In which year was Germany reunited?
29566.e: After the fall of the Wall in 1989 the four victorious powers also agreed. On 3 October 1990 East and West Germany became one state again.

29567.q: Which headquarters did citizens occupy in East Berlin in January 1990?
a: The parliament of the Federal Republic
29567.e: The State Security service had spied on the population for decades. By occupying the building, people wanted to stop the files from being destroyed.
29567.m: The Stasi files were secured by citizens in 1990.

29568.q: Who was the last leader of the Soviet Union?
29568.e: Mikhail Gorbachev resigned as President of the Soviet Union in December 1991. After that the state no longer existed.
29568.m: Gorbachev was the last leader of the Soviet Union.

29569.q: What does the Russian word “perestroika” mean?
29569.e: With perestroika the Soviet leadership wanted to restructure the economy and the state from 1985. But the reforms also shook the whole system.

29570.q: Which politician stood on a tank in Moscow in August 1991 to protest against the coup plotters?
29570.e: From the tank, Boris Yeltsin called for resistance to the coup. After that he became the most powerful politician in Russia.
29570.m: In 1991 Boris Yeltsin defied the coup plotters on a tank.

29571.q: What happened to the Warsaw Pact in 1991?
29571.e: The military alliance of the Eastern Bloc countries was officially dissolved in Prague on 1 July 1991. Many former members later joined NATO.

29572.q: From which country did the Soviet Union withdraw its troops in 1989 after a ten-year war?
29572.e: The Soviet Union had invaded Afghanistan in 1979. The costly war weakened the country and ended with the withdrawal in February 1989.
29572.m: The war in Afghanistan greatly weakened the Soviet Union.

29573.q: What does the abbreviation CIS stand for?
29573.e: The CIS was founded in December 1991 by former Soviet republics. It was meant to ensure cooperation after the end of the Soviet Union.
29573.m: The CIS is the Commonwealth of Independent States.

29574.q: Which three states are called the Baltic states?
29574.e: The three countries on the Baltic Sea were occupied by the Soviet Union in 1940. In 1991 they became independent again.
29574.m: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are the Baltic states.

29575.q: Which US magazine named Gandhi “Man of the Year” for 1930?
29575.e: The news magazine “Time” named Gandhi “Man of the Year” for 1930 because of the Salt March. This made his protest known around the world.
29575.m: The Salt March made Gandhi famous around the world.

29576.q: Which form of struggle did Gandhi stand for in the resistance to British colonial rule?
29576.e: Gandhi relied on non-violent civil disobedience, which he called “Satyagraha”. He wanted to win over his opponents through steadfastness rather than violence.
29576.m: Gandhi fought for India’s freedom without violence.

29577.q: In which country did Gandhi live for over 20 years before returning to India?
29577.e: From 1893 Gandhi worked as a lawyer in South Africa and fought there against discrimination against Indians. In 1915 he returned to India.
29577.m: Gandhi developed his non-violent resistance in South Africa.

29578.q: How did Gandhi break British law at the end of the Salt March?
a: He picked up salt on the beach
He set fire to a customs house
29578.e: On the morning of 6 April 1930 Gandhi picked up a handful of salt on the beach at Dandi. Because only the colonial government was allowed to produce salt, this was a symbolic breaking of the law.
29578.m: A handful of salt became a sign of resistance.

29579.q: How did Gandhi’s followers react in 1930 when the police beat them with sticks?
29579.e: Gandhi taught non-violent resistance. Reports of the beaten but peaceful protesters shocked the whole world.
29579.m: Gandhi’s followers stayed non-violent even when they were beaten.

29580.q: What was Gandhi protesting against with the Salt March?
a: Bread prices that were too high
29580.e: Only the British colonial government was allowed to produce salt, and it charged a tax on it. Because everyone needs salt, this hit even the poorest people.
29580.m: The Salt March was aimed at the British salt tax.

29581.q: Roughly how long was the route of the Salt March?
29581.e: Gandhi and his companions covered about 385 kilometres on foot. The march lasted from 12 March to 5 April 1930, that is 24 days.
29581.m: The Salt March was about 385 kilometres long.

29582.q: How did Gandhi travel the route of the Salt March?
29582.e: Gandhi walked with his companions for 24 days to the sea. Along the way more and more people joined them.
29582.m: Gandhi walked the Salt March on foot.

29583.q: Which symbol is in the middle of the Indian national flag?
29583.e: In the middle of the flag is the blue Ashoka Chakra, a wheel with 24 spokes. The flag was adopted shortly before independence in 1947.
29583.m: The wheel on the Indian flag is called the Ashoka Chakra.

29584.q: Which new state was created alongside India when British India was divided in 1947?
29584.e: British India was divided into mainly Hindu India and mainly Muslim Pakistan. Pakistan became independent one day before India.
29584.m: When British India was divided in 1947, India and Pakistan were created.

29585.q: What does India celebrate every year on 26 January?
a: The constitution coming into force in 1950
The end of the Salt March
29585.e: On 26 January 1950 the Indian constitution came into force and India became a republic. This “Republic Day” is a national holiday.
29585.m: On 26 January India celebrates Republic Day.

29586.q: What did the Muslim League demand before India’s independence?
a: A king for all of India
29586.e: The Muslim League under Muhammad Ali Jinnah wanted a separate state for Muslims. This is how Pakistan was created in 1947.
29586.m: Pakistan was created as a state for the Muslims of British India.

29587.e: India was a British colony. The last British viceroy, Lord Mountbatten, organised the handover of power in 1947.

29588.q: What happened to many millions of people when India was divided in 1947?
29588.e: More than ten million Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims fled across the new borders. Hundreds of thousands of people died in violence during the partition.
29588.m: The partition of India caused a huge wave of refugees.

29589.q: Which present-day country was part of Pakistan as East Pakistan until 1971?
29589.e: From 1947 Pakistan consisted of two parts far apart from each other. The eastern part declared independence as Bangladesh in 1971.
29589.m: Bangladesh used to be called East Pakistan.

29590.q: How did Mahatma Gandhi die in January 1948?
29590.e: On 30 January 1948 a radical Hindu nationalist shot Gandhi in Delhi. The killer rejected Gandhi’s policy of reconciliation with Muslims.
29590.m: Gandhi was murdered a few months after independence.

29591.q: Why is 1960 called the “Year of Africa”?
a: Because many African colonies became independent
Because Africa got its own currency
Because the Olympic Games took place in Africa
Because Africa was fully mapped for the first time
29591.e: In 1960, 18 colonies in Africa became independent, most of them from France. There were never again so many new states in one year.
29591.m: In 1960 many African states became independent.

29592.q: From which colonial power did most African states become independent in 1960?
29592.e: Of the 18 colonies that became free in 1960, 14 belonged to France. They include Senegal, Mali and Cameroon.
29592.m: Most of the states of the Year of Africa were French colonies.

29593.q: Which country with a large population became independent from Great Britain on 1 October 1960?
29593.e: Nigeria gained independence from Great Britain on 1 October 1960. Today it is the country with the largest population in Africa.
29593.m: Nigeria became independent from Great Britain in 1960.

29594.q: Which language is still an official language in many states that became independent from France in 1960?
29594.e: In countries such as Senegal, Mali or Burkina Faso, French remained an official language. People there also speak many African languages.
29594.m: French is spoken in many former French colonies.

29595.q: Which island nation in the Indian Ocean became independent from France in 1960?
29595.e: Madagascar declared independence from France on 26 June 1960. It is the largest island in Africa.

29596.q: Which country south of the Sahara became one of the first to gain independence, as early as 1957?
29596.e: The British colony of the Gold Coast became independent as Ghana in 1957. Its leader Kwame Nkrumah became a role model for other independence movements.
29596.m: Ghana became independent in 1957 and gave other colonies courage.

29597.q: What does it mean when a colony becomes independent?
a: It governs itself as its own state
It is sold to another country
It gets a new king from Europe
It has to pay more taxes to Europe
29597.e: A colony is ruled by a foreign country. When it becomes independent, its own government decides about the country.
29597.m: Independent means a country governs itself.

29598.q: Which organisation did independent African states found in Addis Ababa in 1963?
29598.e: The Organisation of African Unity was meant to promote cooperation between the young states and support decolonisation. In 2002 it was replaced by the African Union.
29598.m: The African Union grew out of the Organisation of African Unity.

29599.q: In which year was Nelson Mandela born?
29599.e: Mandela was born on 18 July 1918 in the village of Mvezo in eastern South Africa. He lived to the age of 95.

29600.q: On which prison island was Mandela held for the longest time?
29600.e: Mandela spent 18 years on Robben Island off Cape Town. Today the island is a museum and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
29600.m: Mandela was imprisoned on Robben Island for a long time.

29601.q: Which party did Nelson Mandela belong to?
29601.e: Mandela was a leading member of the African National Congress (ANC), which fought against apartheid. The ANC was banned from 1960 to 1990.
29601.m: Mandela fought against apartheid in the ANC.

29602.q: Which country did Nelson Mandela come from?
29602.e: Mandela was born in 1918 in a village in eastern South Africa. All his life he fought against racial segregation in his country.
29602.m: Nelson Mandela came from South Africa.

29603.q: How many years in total did Nelson Mandela spend in prison?
29603.e: Mandela was arrested in 1962 and only released in 1990. So he was a prisoner for 27 years, 18 of them on Robben Island.
29603.m: Mandela was in prison for 27 years.

29604.q: Which office did Nelson Mandela take up in 1994?
29604.e: After the first free elections, Mandela became South Africa’s first Black president in 1994. He governed until 1999.
29604.m: In 1994 Mandela became South Africa’s first Black president.

29605.q: What did Nelson Mandela work for after his release in 1990?
a: Reconciliation between Black and white people
29605.e: Even though he had been imprisoned for so long, Mandela did not call for revenge. He wanted everyone in South Africa to live together peacefully.

29606.q: What profession had Nelson Mandela trained for?
29606.e: Mandela studied law and in 1952, with Oliver Tambo, opened the first Black law firm in Johannesburg.
29606.m: Mandela was a lawyer by profession.

29607.e: The word comes from Afrikaans and means something like “separateness”. Black and white people were supposed to live apart.

29608.q: What did apartheid in South Africa require, for example?
a: Separate schools and buses for Black and white people
29608.e: From 1948 racial segregation was expanded by law. Black people were not allowed to use many schools, beaches, buses and residential areas.
29608.m: Apartheid separated Black and white people in almost every area of life.

29609.q: What happened in the South African town of Sharpeville on 21 March 1960?
a: The first free elections took place
29609.e: Police fired on people who were peacefully demonstrating against the pass laws and killed 69 of them. Today 21 March is the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination.
29609.m: The Sharpeville massacre shocked the world in 1960.

29610.q: Which fighter against apartheid spent 27 years in prison and later became President of South Africa?
29610.e: Nelson Mandela was released in 1990. In 1994 he became South Africa’s first Black president.
29610.m: Nelson Mandela became president after 27 years in prison.

29611.q: What did Black South Africans always have to carry with them during apartheid?
29611.e: The pass laws said where Black people were allowed to be. Anyone caught without a valid pass could be arrested.
29611.m: Pass laws limited Black people’s freedom of movement.

29612.q: When were the first free elections for all population groups held in South Africa?
29612.e: On 27 April 1994 all adults were allowed to vote for the first time, whatever their skin colour. Today this day is a public holiday called “Freedom Day”.
29612.m: In 1994 everyone in South Africa could vote for the first time.

29613.q: Which archbishop led the Truth and Reconciliation Commission after apartheid?
29613.e: From 1996 Desmond Tutu led the commission that examined the crimes of the apartheid era. He had already received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984.
29613.m: Desmond Tutu worked for reconciliation in South Africa.

29614.q: How did many countries respond to apartheid in the 1980s?
a: With a war against South Africa
29614.e: Many countries restricted trade with South Africa and excluded it from sporting events. This pressure helped to end apartheid.
29614.m: Sanctions increased the pressure on the apartheid regime.

29615.q: What did Rosa Parks refuse to do on 1 December 1955?
a: Give up her seat on the bus
29615.e: Rosa Parks was told to give up her seat on the bus to a white passenger and refused. She was then arrested.
29615.m: Rosa Parks stayed in her seat on the bus and became famous.

29616.q: In which country did Rosa Parks live?
29616.e: Rosa Parks lived in Montgomery in the state of Alabama in the south of the USA. Strict racial segregation laws applied there.
29616.m: Rosa Parks lived in the south of the USA.

29617.q: What did many Black residents of Montgomery do after Rosa Parks was arrested?
29617.e: With the bus boycott they wanted to end racial segregation. For more than a year they walked or shared lifts until segregation was lifted.
29617.m: After Rosa Parks was arrested, many people boycotted the buses.

29618.q: What did the laws in the south of the USA require at the time of Rosa Parks?
a: The separation of Black and white people
29618.e: Black and white people had to be kept apart in schools, buses and restaurants. The civil rights movement fought against these laws.
29618.m: At that time racial segregation applied in the south of the USA.

29619.q: Which court declared racial segregation on Montgomery’s buses unconstitutional in 1956?
29619.e: In 1956 the US Supreme Court confirmed that separate seating went against the constitution. After that the bus boycott ended.
29619.m: The Supreme Court ended segregation on Montgomery’s buses.

29620.q: Which well-known minister led the bus boycott after Rosa Parks was arrested?
29620.e: The young minister Martin Luther King became known through the Montgomery bus boycott. He became the most important leader of the civil rights movement.
29620.m: Martin Luther King led the Montgomery bus boycott.

29621.q: What did Rosa Parks work for all her life?
29621.e: Rosa Parks was already active in a civil rights organisation before 1955. She fought against segregation and discrimination.
29621.m: Rosa Parks fought for equal rights for Black people.

29622.q: Where did Martin Luther King give his “I have a dream” speech in 1963?
a: In front of the Lincoln Memorial
In front of the White House
At the UN in New York
29622.e: King spoke at the March on Washington on 28 August 1963 in front of the Lincoln Memorial. About 250,000 people listened to him.
29622.m: King gave his famous speech in front of the Lincoln Memorial.

29623.q: What is the core message of King’s “I have a dream” speech?
29623.e: King dreamed that his children would be judged not by the colour of their skin but by their character. The speech became a symbol of the civil rights movement.
29623.m: King dreamed of equal rights for all people.

29624.q: What was the name of Martin Luther King’s wife, who also worked for civil rights?
29624.e: Coretta Scott King married Martin Luther King in 1953. After his death she continued his work for equal rights.
29624.m: Coretta Scott King carried on her husband’s work.

29625.q: What was opened on the National Mall in Washington in 2011 in honour of King?
29625.e: The Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial shows King as a stone figure. It is the first memorial on the National Mall to an African American.
29625.m: Since 2011 there has been a memorial to King on the National Mall.

29626.q: What happened in Memphis on 4 April 1968?
29626.e: Martin Luther King was shot on the balcony of a motel in Memphis. His death led to riots in many US cities.
29626.m: Martin Luther King was murdered in 1968.

29627.q: What did an important law in the USA ban in 1964?
29627.e: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned discrimination because of skin colour, religion or origin. It was a great success for the civil rights movement.
29627.m: In 1964 legal racial segregation was banned in the USA.

29628.q: What were the marches from Selma to Montgomery in 1965 mainly for?
a: The right of Black people to vote
29628.e: In the south, Black people were often prevented from voting. In the same year, 1965, the marches led to the Voting Rights Act, which protected the right to vote.
29628.m: The Selma marches fought for the right to vote.

29629.q: In which year were the Treaties of Rome signed?
29629.e: The Treaties of Rome were signed in Rome on 25 March 1957. They came into force on 1 January 1958.
29629.m: The Treaties of Rome date from 1957.

29630.q: Which community was founded with the Treaties of Rome?
29630.e: The Treaties of Rome founded the European Economic Community (EEC) and the European Atomic Energy Community. The EEC created a common market.
29630.m: The EEC was created with the Treaties of Rome.

29631.q: How many states signed the Treaties of Rome?
29631.e: The founding states were all in Western Europe. They had already founded the European Coal and Steel Community together in 1951.
29631.m: Six states signed the Treaties of Rome.

29632.q: Which country was NOT one of the founding states of the Treaties of Rome?
29632.e: Great Britain only joined the community in 1973, together with Denmark and Ireland. So it was not a founding member.
29632.m: Great Britain was not a founding member of the EEC.

29633.q: In which city do many important institutions of the European Union have their seat?
29633.e: The European Commission and the Council of the EU work in Brussels, the capital of Belgium. That is why Brussels is often called the capital of Europe.
29633.m: Brussels is the centre of the European Union.

29635.q: How did Swiss voters reject closer ties with the EC in 1992?
a: They said no to joining the EEA
They said no to the UN
They said no to the euro
29635.e: On 6 December 1992 the people and the cantons narrowly rejected joining the European Economic Area. Since then Switzerland has managed its relationship with the EU through bilateral agreements.
29635.m: Switzerland is not an EU member and relies on bilateral agreements.

29636.q: Since when have people in the eurozone been able to pay with euro cash?
29636.e: The euro was first introduced in 1999 for non-cash payments. Banknotes and coins have existed since 1 January 2002.

29637.q: Why don’t people in Switzerland pay with the euro?
a: Switzerland has its own currency, the franc.
The euro is banned in Switzerland.
Switzerland has no cash at all.
The euro is only valid in Germany.
29637.e: Switzerland does not belong to the EU or the eurozone. Its currency is the Swiss franc.
29637.m: In Switzerland people pay with francs.

29638.q: In which city does the European Central Bank have its seat?
29638.e: The European Central Bank is responsible for monetary policy in the eurozone. Its seat is in Frankfurt am Main.
29638.m: The European Central Bank is in Frankfurt.

29639.q: Which currency did the euro replace in Germany?
29639.e: In Germany the Deutschmark was replaced by the euro. One euro was worth 1.95583 marks.
29639.m: In Germany the euro replaced the Deutschmark.

29640.q: What do euro banknotes show on the front?
a: Windows and gateways in different architectural styles
The flags of all member countries
29640.e: The banknotes show imaginary windows and gateways from different periods of European architecture. This way no single country is favoured.
29640.m: Euro notes show imaginary buildings from different periods.

29641.q: Which side of a euro coin is different depending on the country it comes from?
29641.e: The side with the value is the same everywhere, but each country designs the back itself. Even so, all coins are valid throughout the eurozone.
29641.m: Euro coins have a national back.

29642.q: Which bank issues banknotes in Switzerland?
29642.e: The Swiss National Bank is responsible for the franc. It issues the banknotes and makes sure the money keeps its value.
29642.m: The National Bank issues Swiss banknotes.

29643.q: Which honour did the inventor of the web, Tim Berners-Lee, receive from the British Queen in 2004?
a: He was given his own island
29643.e: Queen Elizabeth II knighted Berners-Lee for his services to the development of the internet. Since then he has been allowed to use the title “Sir”.
29643.m: Tim Berners-Lee has the title Sir.

a: A program for displaying web pages
A computer that stores web pages
29644.e: With a browser you open web pages and click on links. Well-known browsers today are Chrome, Firefox and Safari.

29646.q: Which language, developed by Berners-Lee, is used to build web pages?
29646.e: HTML stands for “Hypertext Markup Language” and describes the structure of a web page. Berners-Lee developed it together with the transfer protocol HTTP.
29646.m: Web pages are described with HTML.

29647.q: What is the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web?
a: The web is a service on the internet
The internet is part of the web
The web is older than the internet
29647.e: The internet is the worldwide network of connected computers. The World Wide Web is a service on it that offers linked web pages, just like email, for example.
29647.m: The web is just one service on the internet.

29648.q: What was the name of Tim Berners-Lee’s first web browser?
29648.e: In 1990 Berners-Lee programmed the first browser on a NeXT computer and called it “WorldWideWeb”. Later it was renamed “Nexus”.
29648.m: The first browser was called WorldWideWeb.

29649.q: At which address could the very first web page be found?
29649.e: The first web page explained what the World Wide Web is and how to use it. It ran on a computer at CERN and is online again today.
29649.m: The world’s first web page was at info.cern.ch.

29650.q: Which organisation did Tim Berners-Lee found in 1994 to set web standards?
29650.e: The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) develops shared rules such as HTML standards. This is why web pages work in all browsers.
29650.m: The W3C sets standards for the web.

29651.q: One World Trade Center is 1776 feet tall. What does this number remind us of?
a: The year New York was founded
29651.e: In 1776 the USA declared its independence. 1776 feet is about 541 metres.
29651.m: The height of One World Trade Center recalls 1776.

29652.q: Which two skyscrapers in New York were destroyed on 11 September 2001?
a: The towers of the World Trade Center
The Empire State Building and the Chrysler Building
Trump Tower and the Rockefeller Center
The UN headquarters and Wall Street
29652.e: Two aeroplanes crashed into the twin towers of the World Trade Center. Both towers collapsed within two hours.
29652.m: The twin towers of the World Trade Center collapsed in 2001.

29653.q: Which building of the US Department of Defense was hit on 11 September 2001?
29653.e: A hijacked aeroplane crashed into the Pentagon near Washington. The building is the headquarters of the US Department of Defense.
29653.m: On 11 September the Pentagon was hit too.

29654.q: Why did the fourth hijacked plane on 11 September not reach its target?
a: Passengers fought back against the hijackers
It was landed by the police
A thunderstorm took it off course
29654.e: On board United Airlines Flight 93, passengers tried to take back the cockpit. The plane crashed near Shanksville in Pennsylvania.
29654.m: Brave passengers prevented another target from being hit.

29655.q: What is now on the site of the destroyed twin towers?
a: Two large pools as a memorial
29655.e: The “National September 11 Memorial” has two pools in the footprints of the towers. The names of the victims are on their edges.
29655.m: Two pools remind us of the destroyed towers.

29656.q: Roughly how many people died in the attacks of 11 September 2001?
29656.e: 2977 victims died in the attacks, not counting the attackers. It was the deadliest terrorist attack in history.

29657.q: In which country did the USA start a war in October 2001 in response to the attacks?
29657.e: The Taliban in Afghanistan gave al-Qaeda a hiding place. That is why the USA and its allies attacked Afghanistan from October 2001.
29657.m: After 11 September the war in Afghanistan began.

29658.q: Which new government department did the USA create in 2002 after the attacks?
29658.e: The Department of Homeland Security is meant to protect the USA from terrorist attacks and other dangers. It brought together many authorities that had been separate.
29658.m: After 11 September a Department of Homeland Security was created.

29659.q: In which year was the Paris climate agreement adopted?
29659.e: The agreement was adopted on 12 December 2015 at the UN climate conference in Paris. It came into force as early as November 2016.
29659.m: The Paris climate agreement dates from 2015.

29660.q: To how many degrees should global warming be limited if possible, according to the Paris agreement?
29660.e: Warming should stay well below 2 degrees, if possible at 1.5 degrees. This is compared with the time before industrialisation.
29660.m: The Paris goal is warming of only 1.5 degrees if possible.

a: A police force for environmental offenders
A gas that warms the climate
A company that builds solar panels
29661.e: At the COP almost all the countries of the world meet to negotiate on climate protection. The Paris conference in 2015 was COP21.
29661.m: At the COP countries negotiate on climate protection.

29662.q: What do countries in the Paris agreement have to submit regularly?
29662.e: Each country decides for itself how much it wants to cut its greenhouse gases. These climate targets are to be renewed and tightened every five years.
29662.m: In the Paris agreement each country sets its own climate targets.

29663.q: Which greenhouse gas is the Paris agreement mainly meant to reduce?
29663.e: Carbon dioxide (CO2) is produced mainly by burning coal, oil and gas. It is the most important driver of man-made global warming.
29663.m: Less CO2 should slow down global warming.

29664.q: By when does Switzerland want to cut its greenhouse gas emissions to net zero according to its climate law?
29664.e: Swiss voters approved the climate law in June 2023. It states that Switzerland should become climate-neutral by 2050.
29664.m: Switzerland wants to become climate-neutral by 2050.

29665.q: Which country left the Paris agreement under President Trump?
29665.e: The USA left the agreement in 2020 under President Trump and rejoined in 2021. In January 2025 Trump again announced its withdrawal, which took effect in January 2026.
29665.m: The USA left the Paris agreement under Trump.

29666.q: From 2021, what did the WHO use to name important variants of the coronavirus?
29666.e: Variants such as Alpha, Delta or Omicron were given Greek letters. The WHO wanted to avoid countries being stigmatised by variant names.
29666.m: Coronavirus variants were named after Greek letters.

29667.q: In which Chinese city did the first cases of COVID-19 become known at the end of 2019?
29667.e: The first cases were found in Wuhan in December 2019. From there the virus spread around the world.
29667.m: COVID-19 was first discovered in Wuhan.

29668.q: When did the World Health Organization declare COVID-19 a pandemic?
29668.e: The WHO classified the spread as a pandemic on 11 March 2020. A pandemic is a disease that spreads across many countries and continents.
29668.m: The WHO declared the pandemic in March 2020.

29669.q: What does the number “19” in the name COVID-19 stand for?
29669.e: COVID-19 is short for “Coronavirus Disease 2019”. The disease was first discovered in 2019.
29669.m: The 19 in COVID-19 stands for the year 2019.

29670.q: What did the Swiss Covid certificate confirm from 2021?
29670.e: The Covid certificate showed that a person was vaccinated, had recovered or had tested negative. At times it was required for restaurants, events and travel.
29670.m: The Covid certificate confirmed vaccination, recovery or a test.

29671.q: Who decided on the Covid-19 law at the ballot box in Switzerland?
29671.e: A referendum was called against the Covid-19 law. That is why the people voted on it, even three times between 2021 and 2023. Each time the law was approved.
29671.m: In Switzerland the voters decided on the Covid-19 law.

29672.q: Which new technology were the first Covid vaccines approved in Switzerland based on?
29672.e: The first Covid vaccines approved in Switzerland were mRNA vaccines. They give the body building instructions for a protein of the virus so that the immune system can recognise it.
29672.m: mRNA vaccines helped in the fight against COVID-19.

29673.q: When did children in Switzerland go back to state school after the first period of distance learning?
29673.e: From 16 March 2020 children learned at home. On 11 May 2020 the compulsory schools opened again.
29673.m: Swiss state schools reopened in May 2020.

29674.q: In which year did the Helvetii set off from the Swiss Plateau to emigrate to Gaul?
29674.e: In spring 58 BC the Helvetii left their land with allied tribes. Julius Caesar stood in their way.
29674.m: The departure of the Helvetii began in 58 BC.

29675.q: According to Caesar, which rich Helvetian nobleman planned the departure of the Helvetii?
29675.e: Orgetorix persuaded the Helvetii to emigrate. But he died in 60 BC, before the march even began.
29675.m: Orgetorix planned the departure of the Helvetii.

29676.q: According to Caesar, what did the Helvetii do with their towns and villages before they set off?
a: They gave them to the Raetians
29676.e: Caesar reports that they burned their 12 towns and about 400 villages. That way nobody would think of turning back.
29676.m: Before setting off, the Helvetii burned their own settlements.

29677.q: Where did the Helvetii want to go in the year they left?
a: To south-west Gaul by the Atlantic
To northern Italy in the Po valley
29677.e: Their goal was the land of the Santones in the south-west of present-day France. There they hoped for more land and safety.
29677.m: The Helvetii wanted to settle in western Gaul near the Atlantic.

29678.q: Whose account gives us most of what we know about the departure of the Helvetii?
29678.e: Caesar described the campaign himself in his work “De bello Gallico” (The Gallic War). Because he took part in the war himself, his account is not neutral.
29678.m: Julius Caesar is the most important source on the departure of the Helvetii.

29679.q: At which town did Caesar have the bridge over the Rhône destroyed to block the Helvetii’s way?
29679.e: Geneva then belonged to the Allobroges and already lay within Roman power. Caesar had the bridge torn down and the bank of the Rhône fortified.
29679.m: Caesar blocked the Helvetii’s way across the Rhône at Geneva.

29680.q: According to Caesar, how many people set off in total with the Helvetii and their allies?
29680.e: Caesar gives 368,000 people, about 92,000 of them warriors. Experts today think this number is exaggerated.
29680.m: According to Caesar, several hundred thousand people set off with the Helvetii.

29681.q: Why did Caesar force the defeated Helvetii to return to their old homeland?
a: So that no Germanic tribes would take the empty land
So that they would mine gold there for Rome
Because the Romans did not know the land
Because a war against Raetia was starting there
29681.e: An empty Swiss Plateau would have attracted Germanic tribes from across the Rhine. The Helvetii were to act as a buffer and rebuild their settlements.
29681.m: The Helvetii had to return so that their land would not fall into Germanic hands.

29682.q: In which present-day country is the site of the Battle of Bibracte?
29682.e: Bibracte lay in what is now the region of Burgundy in France. So the Helvetii were already far from their homeland.
29682.m: The Battle of Bibracte took place in present-day France.

29683.q: Who won the Battle of Bibracte?
29683.e: Caesar’s legions defeated the Helvetii after a long, hard fight. That meant the departure had failed.
29683.m: At Bibracte the Romans under Caesar defeated the Helvetii.

29684.q: Which people from the area of present-day Switzerland were defeated at Bibracte?
29684.e: The Helvetii had emigrated in 58 BC. At Bibracte they were defeated by Caesar.
29684.m: At Bibracte the Helvetii were defeated by the Romans.

29685.q: Why did the Helvetii leave their homeland before the Battle of Bibracte?
a: They were looking for new, better land
A volcano had destroyed their land
They wanted to sail across the sea
29685.e: The Helvetii wanted to move to western Gaul, where they hoped for more space. Caesar stood in their way.
29685.m: The Helvetii set off to find new land.

29686.e: Oppida were large Celtic settlements protected by ramparts and walls. Caesar used this Latin word for them.
29686.m: An oppidum is a fortified Celtic town.

29687.q: What did the Helvetii have to do after their defeat at Bibracte?
29687.e: Caesar sent the survivors back to their homeland. There they were to rebuild their destroyed villages.
29687.m: After Bibracte the Helvetii had to go home.

29688.q: What did the Helvetii do with their villages before they left?
a: They sold them to the Romans
They gave them to the Germanic tribes
29688.e: According to Caesar the Helvetii burned down their towns and villages. That way there was no going back for them.
29688.m: Before leaving, the Helvetii burned down their villages.

29689.e: A villa rustica was a farm with a house, stables and storehouses. There were hundreds of them on the Swiss Plateau.
29689.m: A villa rustica was a Roman farm in the countryside.

29690.q: What belonged to a villa rustica?
29690.e: A villa rustica was a Roman farm. Besides the owner’s house there were stables, workshops and storehouses.
29690.m: A villa rustica was a Roman farm with many buildings.

29691.q: How were some rooms heated in grand Roman country estates?
29691.e: In hypocaust heating, hot air from a fire flowed under the floor and through the walls. For this the floor rested on small brick pillars.
29691.m: The Romans heated rooms with underfloor heating, the hypocaust.

29692.q: What did Roman country estates in Switzerland mainly produce?
29692.e: The estates grew grain and kept livestock. They sold what they did not need to towns and to the army.
29692.m: Roman country estates mainly supplied the land with food.

29693.q: What is the Roman country estate of Orbe-Boscéaz in the canton of Vaud especially famous for?
29693.e: Several magnificent mosaic floors survive at Orbe-Boscéaz. They show gods and animals, for example.
29693.m: The estate at Orbe is famous for its beautiful mosaics.

29694.q: What were the roofs of Roman country estates usually covered with?
29694.e: The Romans brought roof tiles of fired clay to our region. Flat tiles and round curved tiles were used together.
29694.m: Roman country estates had roofs of fired tiles.

29695.q: What hit many Roman country estates in Switzerland hard from the middle of the 3rd century?
a: A volcanic eruption in the Jura
29695.e: Around AD 260 the Alemanni pushed across the Rhine and plundered. Many estates got destroyed or abandoned.
29695.m: Germanic raids brought many estates to an end.

29696.q: Which people lived in the alpine valleys of present-day Grisons before the Romans?
29696.e: The Raetians were an alpine people with their own language and script. The Roman province was named after them.
29696.m: The Raetians lived in the Grisons before Roman times.

29697.q: In which year did the Romans conquer the Raetians in a great alpine campaign?
29697.e: Emperor Augustus wanted to secure the alpine passes. In 15 BC his troops conquered the alpine region as far as the Danube.
29697.m: The Roman alpine campaign took place in 15 BC.

29698.q: Which Roman emperor had the alpine peoples conquered in 15 BC?
29698.e: Emperor Augustus wanted to secure the alpine passes. His stepsons led the campaign against the Raetians.
29698.m: Emperor Augustus had the Alps conquered.

29699.q: Which people was the Roman province of Raetia named after?
29699.e: The Raetians lived in the alpine valleys. The Romans named the new province after them.
29699.m: Raetia is named after the Raetians.

29700.q: Which Swiss national language goes back to the everyday Latin of the province of Raetia?
29700.e: The people took on the Latin of the Romans. Over centuries this developed into Romansh in the Grisons.
29700.m: Romansh developed from the Latin of the province of Raetia.

29701.q: Which town in the Grisons was already important in Roman times and was then called Curia?
29701.e: Chur is one of the oldest towns in Switzerland. In late antiquity it served as the capital of a Roman province and later became the seat of a bishop.

29702.q: What did the Romans build to celebrate their victory over the alpine peoples?
29702.e: The victory monument Tropaeum Alpium stands in La Turbie near Monaco. Its inscription names 46 conquered alpine peoples.
29702.m: A Roman victory monument recalls the conquest of the Alps.

29703.q: Lousonna is the Roman settlement that came before which present-day city?
29703.e: The name Lousonna is recorded in inscriptions. The present-day place name Lausanne developed from it.
29703.m: The name Lausanne came from the Roman Lousonna.

29704.q: Which language did the Romans speak in Lousonna?
29704.e: In Roman times Latin served as the language of government and trade. French later developed from everyday Latin.
29704.m: In Roman times people in Lousonna spoke Latin.

29705.q: On which lake did the Roman settlement of Lousonna lie?
29705.e: Lousonna lay right on the northern shore of Lake Geneva. Its position by the water was very good for trade.
29705.m: Lousonna was a Roman settlement on Lake Geneva.

29706.q: What did Lousonna have right on the lake shore?
29706.e: There was a harbour on the shore. An inscription by boatmen shows that goods were transported by water.
29706.m: Lousonna had a harbour for trade.

29707.q: What kind of settlement was Lousonna in Roman times?
a: A small town with a harbour
29707.e: Lousonna, a Roman vicus on Lake Geneva, had a harbour, a market and temples. A few thousand people lived there.
29707.m: Lousonna: a small Roman town on the lake.

29708.q: Where did the settlement move to when things became unsafe from the late 3rd century?
a: To an island in the lake
Into the Rhône valley to Sion
29708.e: Because of Germanic raids, people moved further up to a safe place. This became the medieval bishop’s town of Lausanne.
29708.m: For safety, the people of Lousonna moved up onto the hill.

29709.q: Which international organisation has its headquarters today on the site of the former Lousonna?
29709.e: The IOC headquarters, Olympic House, stands in Vidy. Parts of the Roman settlement used to lie there.
29709.m: The International Olympic Committee is based on the ground of old Lousonna.

29710.q: Which two areas does the Great St Bernard Pass connect?
29710.e: The pass road leads from the Rhône valley through the Val d’Entremont over into the Italian Aosta Valley. The Romans already used this route to Gaul.
29710.m: The Great St Bernard connects Valais with the Aosta Valley.

29711.q: Roughly how high is the top of the Great St Bernard Pass?
29711.e: The top of the pass is 2,469 metres above sea level. In winter the road is closed because of snow.
29711.m: The Great St Bernard is almost 2,500 metres high.

29712.q: Which people built a road for vehicles over the Great St Bernard almost 2,000 years ago?
29712.e: Before that you could only cross the pass with pack animals. In the 1st century AD the Romans widened the road for carts.
29712.m: The Romans made the Great St Bernard passable for vehicles.

29713.q: To which chief Roman god was the temple at the top of the Great St Bernard Pass dedicated?
29713.e: The Celts worshipped the god Poeninus on the pass. The Romans linked him with their chief god Jupiter.
29713.m: At the top of the pass stood a Roman temple to Jupiter.

29714.q: Which town in Valais at the foot of the Great St Bernard was an important place with an amphitheatre in Roman times?
29714.e: Martigny counted as the most important Roman place in Valais. An amphitheatre and the remains of a temple still survive there.
29714.m: Martigny: the main Roman town at the foot of the Great St Bernard.

29715.q: Which town on the south side of the pass was called Augusta Praetoria in Roman times?
29715.e: Augusta Praetoria got founded around 25 BC. The name Aosta developed from “Augusta”.
29715.m: Aosta: the Roman town at the southern foot of the Great St Bernard.

29716.q: What were the stone pillars called that showed distances along Roman roads like the one over the Great St Bernard?
29716.e: Milestones gave the distance to the next important place and often the emperor’s name. Some stand in museums today.
29716.m: Milestones showed distances along Roman roads.

29717.q: When did the Alemanni begin to settle permanently on the Swiss Plateau?
29717.e: After the end of Roman rule, the Alemanni gradually moved across the Rhine. They settled first in northern Switzerland and then further south.
29717.m: The Alemanni settled the Swiss Plateau in the 5th and 6th centuries.

29718.q: Which place-name ending is typical of early Alemannic settlements in German-speaking Switzerland?
29718.e: The ending means something like “among the people of ...” and points to a clan. Examples are Ossingen, Beringen and Hettlingen.
29718.m: The ending -ingen often reveals an early Alemannic settlement.

29719.q: Which group of dialects does Swiss German belong to?
29719.e: The dialects of German-speaking Switzerland go back to the language of the Alemanni. People in Alsace and southern Baden also speak Alemannic.
29719.m: Swiss German is an Alemannic dialect.

29720.q: Which people did the Alemanni have to submit to around AD 500?
29720.e: The Frankish king Clovis defeated the Alemanni in several battles. After that their land belonged to the Frankish kingdom.
29720.m: Around 500 the Alemanni came under Frankish rule.

29721.q: What happened when the Romans withdrew many soldiers from the Rhine border around AD 400?
a: The Alemanni moved more easily into northern Switzerland
The Vikings occupied the Swiss Plateau
29721.e: The Romans needed the soldiers to defend Italy. After that the way across the Rhine lay more open for the Alemanni.
29721.m: After the Romans withdrew, the Alemanni came to northern Switzerland.

29722.q: What religion did the Alemanni have when they settled in northern Switzerland?
29722.e: At first the Alemanni worshipped Germanic gods such as Woden. Only in the 7th and 8th centuries did they gradually become Christians.
29722.m: The early Alemanni believed in Germanic gods.

29723.q: Which finds tell archaeologists most about the early Alemanni in Switzerland?
29723.e: The Alemanni buried their dead in rows of graves with weapons, jewellery and tools. These grave goods show how they lived.
29723.m: Alemannic cemeteries are an important source for the early Middle Ages.

29724.q: Which Germanic people settled in what is now western Switzerland in the 5th century?
29724.e: In 443 the Romans gave the Burgundians land in Sapaudia, in present-day western Switzerland and Savoy. They were meant to protect the border there.
29724.m: The Burgundians settled in western Switzerland in the 5th century.

29725.q: Which area belonged to the Kingdom of Upper Burgundy, founded in 888?
a: Large parts of present-day western Switzerland
29725.e: Rudolph I had himself crowned in 888 in the Abbey of Saint-Maurice. His kingdom covered large parts of present-day western Switzerland.
29725.m: The Kingdom of Upper Burgundy lay in present-day western Switzerland.

29726.q: What did the Burgundian king Gundobad have written down around AD 500?
29726.e: The law of the Burgundians is called the Lex Burgundionum. It set out how Burgundians and Romans lived together.
29726.m: King Gundobad had the law of the Burgundians written down.

29727.q: What happened to the language of the Burgundians in western Switzerland?
a: They took on the Latin of the locals
They spread their Germanic language everywhere
They took on the Raetian language
29727.e: The Burgundians were few and lived among many Romanised locals. They gave up their Germanic language; the French of Romandy later developed from this.
29727.m: The Burgundians adapted and soon spoke a Romance language.

29728.q: Which people conquered the first kingdom of the Burgundians in 534?
29728.e: The sons of Clovis defeated the Burgundians and made their kingdom part of the Frankish kingdom. But the name Burgundy remained.
29728.m: In 534 the Burgundian kingdom fell to the Franks.

29729.q: How does the Burgundian Queen Bertha live on in the legends of western Switzerland?
29729.e: Queen Bertha married King Rudolph II. The saying “au temps où la reine Berthe filait” (in the days when Queen Bertha spun) recalls her as the good old days.
29729.m: Queen Bertha is a popular legendary figure in Romandy.

29730.q: Which empire did Burgundy belong to after the death of King Rudolph III in 1032?
29730.e: After Rudolph III died, the German Emperor Conrad II took over the Kingdom of Burgundy. So western Switzerland also belonged to the Empire.
29730.m: From 1032 Burgundy belonged to the Holy Roman Empire.

29731.q: Which river is seen as the symbol of the German-French language border in Switzerland?
29731.e: The Saane (in French Sarine) flows through the canton of Fribourg. It symbolically separates German-speaking Switzerland from Romandy.
29731.m: The Saane stands as a symbol of the language border.

29732.q: What is the border between German-speaking Switzerland and Romandy jokingly called?
29732.e: The term means “rösti ditch” and refers to rösti, which is seen as typical of German-speaking Switzerland. People often use it when the two parts of the country vote differently.
29732.m: The language border is jokingly called the Röstigraben.

29733.q: Which Swiss town is officially bilingual in German and French?
29733.e: In Biel/Bienne, street signs, authorities and schools are bilingual. Many people switch between the two languages in everyday life.
29733.m: Biel/Bienne is the largest bilingual town in Switzerland.

29734.q: How many Swiss cantons are officially bilingual in German and French?
29734.e: They are the cantons of Bern, Fribourg and Valais. The Grisons is trilingual, with German, Romansh and Italian.
29734.m: Bern, Fribourg and Valais are bilingual cantons.

29735.q: In which part of Valais do most people speak French?
29735.e: In the lower, western part of Valais people mainly speak French. In Upper Valais, which includes the Goms and the Saas valley, people speak German.
29735.m: In Lower Valais people speak French, in Upper Valais German.

29736.q: How did the German-French language border in Switzerland come about?
29736.e: In the early Middle Ages the language of the Alemanni spread, while in the west people spoke a Romance language. So the border gradually took shape.
29736.m: The language border grew over centuries.

29737.q: Which small town in the canton of Fribourg is mainly German-speaking?
29737.e: Murten (in French Morat) lies close to the language border. Most of its people speak German.
29737.m: Murten is a German-speaking town in the bilingual canton of Fribourg.

29738.q: On which day is St Gall’s Day celebrated?
29738.e: St Gall’s Day marks the day the saint died. In the past it was an important date in the countryside, for example for markets and paying interest.
29738.m: St Gall’s Day is on 16 October.

29739.q: According to tradition, which country did the monk Gallus come from?
29739.e: According to tradition Gallus came from Ireland. As a monk he travelled through France as far as Lake Constance.
29739.m: According to tradition Gallus came from Ireland.

29740.q: How did Gallus live in the area of present-day St Gallen?
a: As a hermit in a cell in the forest
As a king in a castle
As a trader in a town
As a farmer on a big farm
29740.e: Gallus built himself a simple cell in the forest and lived there as a hermit. The town of St Gallen later grew from this place.
29740.m: Gallus lived as a hermit in the forest.

29741.q: According to tradition, how did Columbanus and Gallus deal with the pagan idols of the Alemanni?
a: They put them up in churches
29741.e: The accounts of their lives report that Gallus destroyed idols in Tuggen and Bregenz or threw them into the lake. This turned the locals against the monks.
29741.m: Gallus fought against the old Alemannic belief in gods.

29742.q: According to legend, which animal brought Gallus wood while he was building his cell?
29742.e: Gallus is said to have told the animal to put wood on the fire and given it bread in return. That is why the coat of arms of the city of St Gallen shows this animal.
29742.m: According to legend a bear helped St Gallus.

29743.q: What was founded at the grave of Gallus in 719?
29743.e: The priest Otmar founded a monastery at the grave of Gallus. The town of St Gallen later grew up around the monastery.
29743.m: The Abbey of St Gall grew up at the grave of Gallus.

29744.q: What in St Gallen is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
a: The Abbey District with cathedral and library
29744.e: The Abbey District is the former monastery of Gallus. With the cathedral and the famous Abbey Library, it has been a World Heritage Site since 1983.
29744.m: The Abbey District of St Gallen is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

29745.q: Who ruled large areas of present-day eastern Switzerland from the Abbey of St Gall until 1798?
29745.e: The abbot of St Gall also ruled as a worldly lord. That is why he was called the Prince-Abbot. In 1805 the monastery was dissolved.
29745.m: The Prince-Abbot of St Gall ruled over large parts of eastern Switzerland.

29746.q: Which building on the Plan of St Gall is drawn largest and most precisely?
29746.e: The church forms the centre of the whole complex. It is drawn especially carefully, with altars and measurements.
29746.m: The great church stands at the centre of the monastery plan.

29747.q: Around which year was the Plan of St Gall made?
29747.e: Experts date the plan to about 819 to 837, usually around 825/826. So it comes from the Carolingian period.
29747.m: The monastery plan comes from the early 9th century.

29748.q: What material is the Plan of St Gall drawn on?
29748.e: The plan consists of five pieces of parchment, that is treated animal skin, sewn together. It measures about 112 by 77 centimetres.
29748.m: The monastery plan is drawn on parchment.

29749.q: Roughly how many buildings are drawn on the Plan of St Gall?
29749.e: The plan contains floor plans of about 50 buildings with 333 labels. The complex would have had room for over 100 monks.
29749.m: About fifty buildings can be seen on the monastery plan.

29750.q: How is the cemetery designed on the Plan of St Gall?
29750.e: Fruit trees are drawn between the graves. In this way the plan links the place of the dead with a picture of the garden of paradise.
29750.m: On the monastery plan the cemetery is also an orchard.

29751.q: What was the Plan of St Gall meant for?
a: As a model for an ideal monastery
As a map of eastern Switzerland
As a plan for building a castle
As a street map of St Gallen
29751.e: The plan shows what a perfect monastery with a church, workshops, gardens and stables could look like. But it was never built exactly like this.
29751.m: The monastery plan shows an ideal monastery.

29752.q: Roughly how old is the Abbey of Saint-Maurice in Valais?
29752.e: The abbey was founded in 515. In 2015 it celebrated 1,500 years.
29752.m: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice is over 1,500 years old.

29753.q: In which canton is the Abbey of Saint-Maurice?
29753.e: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice lies in the Rhône valley in the canton of Valais. It was founded in 515.
29753.m: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice is in Valais.

29754.q: Which saint is the Abbey of Saint-Maurice named after?
29754.e: Maurice and his soldiers are said to have died as martyrs here. The French name Maurice comes from the Latin Mauritius.
29754.m: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice bears the name of St Maurice.

29755.q: According to the legend of Saint-Maurice, who was St Maurice?
29755.e: According to legend, Maurice led a Roman troop. He and his soldiers are said to have been killed because, as Christians, they would not obey.
29755.m: According to legend, Maurice was a Roman soldier and a Christian.

29756.q: Who had a post at Saint-Maurice long before the monastery?
29756.e: The Romans had a customs and military post here at a narrow point in the Rhône valley. The place was called Agaunum then.
29756.m: Saint-Maurice was already an important place in Roman times.

29757.q: What is the Abbey of Saint-Maurice especially known for?
a: Oldest continuously existing monastery in the West
29757.e: Since it was founded, a religious community has lived at Saint-Maurice without a break. Today it is the Augustinian Canons.
29757.m: Saint-Maurice is seen as the oldest continuously inhabited monastery in the West.

29758.q: What did the monks at Saint-Maurice once do day and night without stopping?
29758.e: The monks took turns in groups, so that singing and prayer in praise of God never stopped. This was called laus perennis.
29758.m: At Saint-Maurice monks once sang and prayed without a break.

29759.q: Which neighbouring country borders the Val Müstair, where St John’s Abbey lies?
29759.e: The Val Müstair lies at the far eastern end of Switzerland. Just after the village of Müstair, South Tyrol begins, which belongs to Italy.
29759.m: Müstair Abbey lies close to the border with Italy.

29761.q: According to tradition, which ruler founded Müstair Abbey?
29761.e: Legend says Charlemagne founded the abbey. A life-size statue of him stands in the church.
29761.m: Charlemagne is seen as the founder of Müstair Abbey.

29762.q: What is the abbey church of Müstair world-famous for?
a: The largest stained-glass windows in Europe
29762.e: Many frescoes with scenes from the Carolingian period survive in the church. There are hardly so many early wall paintings anywhere else.
29762.m: Müstair has unique wall paintings from the Carolingian period.

29763.q: How were experts able to work out the exact founding date of Müstair Abbey?
a: From the tree rings in the building timber
From a coin in the foundations
From an inscription on the doorway
29763.e: Dendrochronology compares the width of the tree rings in wood with known patterns. That way you know when a tree was cut down.
29763.m: Tree rings in wood reveal the age of buildings.

29764.q: Who lives in St John’s Abbey in Müstair today?
29764.e: At first the abbey was a monastery for men. Since the 12th century nuns have lived there following the Rule of St Benedict.
29764.m: Benedictine nuns live in Müstair today.

29765.q: What is housed today in the medieval Planta Tower of Müstair Abbey?
29765.e: The tower was built around 960 and later extended by Abbess Angelina von Planta. Today the abbey museum there shows the history of the abbey.
29765.m: The Planta Tower houses the Müstair Abbey museum.

29766.q: Which hermit lived in the 9th century in the Dark Forest, where Einsiedeln Abbey later grew up?
29766.e: Meinrad was a monk from Reichenau who withdrew into solitude. He is seen as the spiritual founder of Einsiedeln.
29766.m: St Meinrad lived as a hermit where Einsiedeln Abbey later stood.

29767.q: How did the hermit Meinrad die?
29767.e: Two robbers killed Meinrad in 861. Since then he has been honoured as a martyr.

29768.q: According to legend, which animals followed Meinrad’s murderers?
29768.e: The birds gave away the killers, who were then caught. That is why the abbey and the village of Einsiedeln have these animals on their coat of arms.
29768.m: Two ravens are the heraldic animals of Einsiedeln.

29769.q: Which monastic rule do the monks of Einsiedeln Abbey live by?
29769.e: In 934 Eberhard from Strasbourg gathered the hermits into a community following Benedict’s rule. Einsiedeln is still a Benedictine monastery today.

29770.q: Who destroyed the Chapel of Grace in Einsiedeln in 1798?
29770.e: When the French marched into Switzerland in 1798, the chapel got torn down. It got rebuilt from 1815 to 1817.
29770.m: The Chapel of Grace in Einsiedeln was destroyed in 1798 and later rebuilt.

29771.q: In which architectural style was Einsiedeln Abbey rebuilt from 1704?
29771.e: Brother Caspar Moosbrugger planned the huge Baroque complex. The abbey church was consecrated in 1735.
29771.m: Einsiedeln Abbey is a Baroque building.

29772.q: Who attacked Einsiedeln Abbey in January 1314 in the so-called March Dispute?
29772.e: Schwyz and the abbey argued for a long time about pastures and forests. In 1314 men from Schwyz plundered the abbey and took monks prisoner.
29772.m: In the March Dispute, Schwyz and Einsiedeln Abbey fought over land.

29773.q: Through which narrow gorge in the canton of Uri does the route to the Gotthard lead?
29773.e: Only a bridge in the Schöllenen Gorge made the Gotthard route passable. According to legend, the Devil built the Devil’s Bridge.
29773.m: The route to the Gotthard leads through the Schöllenen Gorge.

29774.q: What already stood at the top of the Gotthard Pass in the Middle Ages to take in travellers?
29774.e: A hospice is a simple inn for travellers. On the Gotthard, muleteers and pilgrims found shelter there from cold and storms.
29774.m: On the Gotthard a hospice gave travellers shelter.

29775.q: Which big trading city in northern Italy could traders from the north reach especially directly over the Gotthard?
